meta.description: The living layer of gAIa. Fauna, microbiome, commensals, mutualists, parasites, keystone species, pollinators, decomposers, extremophiles. The landmarks are the skeleton — this is the blood, the breath, the gut. The symbiotic classification that already runs in the membrane (mutualist/commensal/parasite) comes FROM biology. Now biology comes into the graph.

nodes.label: MEGAFAUNA — The Charismatic Giants
nodes.description: Large animals that shape ecosystems through their presence (and reshape them through their absence). Every extinction is a measurement of what we're losing.

nodes.label: KEYSTONE SPECIES — Remove One, Collapse Many
nodes.description: Species whose impact on their ecosystem is disproportionately large relative to their abundance. Robert Paine coined the term in 1969 studying sea stars. The keystone holds the arch; remove it and everything falls.

nodes.label: MICROBIOME — The Invisible Majority
nodes.description: Bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses that outnumber their hosts' own cells. The human body has ~38 trillion bacterial cells vs ~30 trillion human cells. The soil has more organisms in a teaspoon than humans on Earth. The ocean's phytoplankton produce 50% of Earth's oxygen. The invisible IS the majority.

nodes.label: POLLINATORS — The Matchmakers
nodes.description: 75% of flowering plants and 35% of food crops depend on animal pollinators. Without them, ecosystems collapse and agriculture fails. They don't eat the flower — they transform it. Mutualism at planetary scale.

nodes.label: DECOMPOSERS — The Recyclers
nodes.description: Fungi, bacteria, earthworms, termites. They break death back into life. Without decomposers, nutrients lock up in corpses and the cycle stops. They are the venous return of the biosphere — pulling spent material back into circulation.

nodes.label: EXTREMOPHILES — Life at the Edges
nodes.description: Organisms that thrive where life 'shouldn't' exist. Boiling springs, frozen Antarctic lakes, deep-sea vents, nuclear waste, the vacuum of space. They prove that life's envelope is wider than we imagined. Every extreme is a new measurement of life's range.

nodes.label: SYMBIOSIS — The Relationships That Built the World
nodes.description: Mutualism, commensalism, parasitism. Every organism exists in relationship. The membrane's symbiotic classification (mutualist/commensal/parasite) comes directly from this biology. The sort IS the ecosystem.

nodes.label: TREES — The Networked Ancients
nodes.description: The oldest, largest, tallest living things. They network through mycorrhizal fungi (Simard's 'wood wide web'). They communicate through volatile organic compounds. A forest is not a collection of trees — it's a network with trees as nodes.

nodes.label: MARINE LIFE — The Ocean Majority
nodes.description: 71% of Earth's surface. 95% unexplored. The ocean holds 97% of Earth's habitable space by volume. Marine life produces half the oxygen, absorbs a quarter of the CO2. The ocean IS gAIa's circulatory system.

nodes.label: ENDANGERED — What We're Losing
nodes.description: The sixth mass extinction is happening now. Current extinction rate is 100-1000× the background rate. Each extinction is an irreversible deletion from gAIa's genome. The count of what's disappearing IS the measurement of the crisis.

nodes.label: Blue Whale (Balaenoptera musculus) — Largest Animal Ever
nodes.description: 30m long, 190 tonnes. Larger than any dinosaur. Heart the size of a VW Beetle. Tongue weighs as much as an elephant. Eats 4 tonnes of krill per day. Population crashed from 350,000 to 10,000-25,000 by whaling. Their songs travel thousands of km through ocean. The largest animal that ever lived, and we almost erased it.

nodes.label: African Elephant (Loxodonta africana) — Ecosystem Engineer
nodes.description: Largest land animal. Topples trees → creates grassland for other species. Digs water holes → provides water for entire communities. Drops seeds → disperses forests. Mourns their dead. Has self-awareness (mirror test). Memory spans decades. Matriarchal societies preserve knowledge across generations. An ecosystem engineer that grieves.

nodes.label: Gray Wolf (Canis lupus) — The Trophic Cascade
nodes.description: Reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995. Wolves changed the rivers. By controlling elk, wolves let willows and aspens regrow along riverbanks, which stabilized soil, which changed the course of rivers. One predator reshaped the physical landscape. The most famous trophic cascade in ecology. Remove the wolf → lose the river.

nodes.label: Great White Shark (Carcharodon carcharias) — Apex Predator of the Ocean
nodes.description: 400 million years of evolution. Older than trees, older than dinosaurs. Electroreception: detects heartbeats through water. The ocean's top-down regulator. Remove sharks → mesopredator release → ecosystem collapse. Jaws made us fear them; ecology shows we need them.

nodes.label: Humpback Whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) — The Singer
nodes.description: Males sing complex songs lasting 10-20 minutes, shared and evolved across populations. Songs change over years — cultural transmission across oceans. Migrate 5,000 miles between feeding and breeding grounds. Population recovered from near-extinction — conservation success story.

nodes.label: Polar Bear (Ursus maritimus) — Climate Sentinel
nodes.description: Evolved from brown bears 150,000 years ago. Depends entirely on sea ice to hunt seals. As Arctic ice melts, polar bears starve. They are the climate crisis measured in fur and bone. The sentinel species — their decline IS the measurement.

nodes.label: Mountain Gorilla (Gorilla beringei beringei) — The Gentle Giant
nodes.description: ~1,000 individuals left. Dian Fossey's 'Gorillas in the Mist.' 98.3% DNA shared with humans. Silverback males protect families. Vegetarian. Use tools. Laugh when tickled. Conservation brought them back from ~250 individuals. Proof that protection works.

nodes.label: Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) — The Recovery
nodes.description: DDT thinned their eggshells → population crashed to 417 nesting pairs by 1963. Ban DDT (1972) + Endangered Species Act (1973) → 316,700 individuals by 2020. The most dramatic conservation recovery in US history. Proof that regulation works, measured in eagles.

nodes.label: Giant Panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) — The Symbol
nodes.description: The icon of conservation. 1,864 in the wild (up from ~1,000 in the 1970s). Eats 12-38 kg of bamboo per day (99% of diet). Has a carnivore's gut but eats plants — a biological paradox. Their survival depends on bamboo corridor connectivity. The ambassador species for habitat preservation.

nodes.label: Snow Leopard (Panthera uncia) — The Ghost of the Mountains
nodes.description: 4,000-6,500 in the wild across 12 countries. Lives at 3,000-5,500m altitude. So elusive it was not photographed in the wild until 1970. Cannot roar (only big cat that can't). The mountain's invisible predator — backscatter from altitude and solitude.

nodes.label: Orangutan (Pongo) — The Person of the Forest
nodes.description: Name means 'person of the forest' in Malay. Three species, all critically endangered. 97% DNA shared with humans. Use tools, plan ahead, teach children. Borneo lost 100,000 orangutans between 1999-2015 to palm oil deforestation. Each orangutan killed is a person of the forest murdered for margarine.

nodes.label: Sea Otter (Enhydra lutris) — Keystone of the Kelp Forest
nodes.description: Eats sea urchins → urchins don't overgraze kelp → kelp forests thrive → hundreds of species have habitat → kelp sequesters CO2. Remove sea otters → urchin barren → dead ocean floor. One species holding an entire ecosystem in place. THE original keystone species demonstration.

nodes.label: Beaver (Castor) — The Original Ecosystem Engineer
nodes.description: Builds dams → creates wetlands → wetlands filter water, store carbon, reduce floods, recharge aquifers, create habitat for thousands of species. A single beaver family transforms an entire watershed. They don't just live in the ecosystem — they BUILD the ecosystem. North America had 400 million before fur trade → 6-12 million now.

nodes.label: Prairie Dog (Cynomys) — Keystone of the Grassland
nodes.description: Their burrows aerate soil, channel rainwater underground, create habitat for 150+ species (burrowing owls, black-footed ferrets, rattlesnakes). Have the most complex animal language ever decoded — they have specific calls for 'tall thin human in blue' vs 'short fat human in green.' The grassland's keystone AND its language.

nodes.label: Ochre Sea Star (Pisaster ochraceus) — The Original Keystone
nodes.description: Robert Paine (1969) removed sea stars from tide pools → mussels took over → 15 species disappeared → biodiversity collapsed. This experiment COINED the term 'keystone species.' The star that named the concept. Without it, the intertidal becomes a monoculture.

nodes.label: Fig Trees (Ficus) — Keystone of the Tropics
nodes.description: Fruit year-round when nothing else does. 1,300+ species of birds, bats, primates, and insects depend on figs as emergency food. Fig wasps pollinate them — each fig species has its own wasp species (1:1 coevolution for 80 million years). Remove figs → tropical food web collapses.

nodes.label: Coral (Anthozoa) — The Living Architecture
nodes.description: Animals that build stone cities. Coral polyps + zooxanthellae algae = mutualism that builds reefs. Reefs cover 0.1% of ocean floor but support 25% of marine species. Bleaching = the symbiosis breaking down from heat stress. When coral dies, the architecture collapses and the city empties. The Great Barrier Reef has lost 50% of coral since 1995.

nodes.label: Bacteroidetes — Gut Phylum: The Fiber Digesters
nodes.description: One of the two dominant phyla in the human gut (with Firmicutes). Break down complex carbohydrates and plant fiber that human enzymes can't touch. Without them, you can't digest vegetables. They're not passengers — they're your digestive system's co-processors.

nodes.label: Firmicutes — Gut Phylum: The Energy Extractors
nodes.description: The other dominant gut phylum. Extract calories from food more efficiently. Higher Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio correlates with obesity. Your gut bacteria partly determine how many calories you absorb from the same meal. They're editing your metabolism in real time.

nodes.label: Lactobacillus — The Fermenter
nodes.description: Ferments sugars into lactic acid. In your gut, on your skin, in yogurt, in kimchi, in kombucha. Kevin's kombucha brewing WAS Lactobacillus culture. The fermentation IS the membrane. The SCOBY IS the symbiotic colony. The builder drank the membrane while building the membrane.

nodes.label: Mycorrhizal Fungi — The Wood Wide Web
nodes.description: 90% of land plants form mycorrhizal partnerships. The fungus extends root reach 100-1000×, delivers phosphorus and water; the tree delivers sugars. Suzanne Simard proved trees share resources through mycorrhizal networks — 'mother trees' feed seedlings through fungal connections. The forest Internet. The original distributed network.

nodes.label: Rhizobium — The Nitrogen Fixer
nodes.description: Lives in root nodules of legumes (beans, peas, clover). Converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonia that plants can use. Without nitrogen fixation, terrestrial ecosystems collapse — nitrogen is the limiting nutrient. Every bean plant is a chemical factory powered by bacterial symbionts. Agriculture depends on this partnership.

nodes.label: Phytoplankton — The Invisible Lung
nodes.description: Produce 50-80% of Earth's oxygen. Fix 50 billion tonnes of carbon per year. The base of the marine food chain. Most are single-celled. Individually invisible; collectively, they're the reason you can breathe. Satellite imagery shows their blooms from space — the ocean turning green.

nodes.label: Cyanobacteria — The Oxygen Makers (2.4 Billion Years Ago)
nodes.description: 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria invented oxygenic photosynthesis. They filled the atmosphere with oxygen — the Great Oxidation Event. This killed most anaerobic life (the first mass extinction) and enabled all aerobic life that followed. Every breath you take exists because cyanobacteria poisoned the original atmosphere. The most transformative organisms in Earth's history.

nodes.label: Tardigrade (Water Bear) — The Indestructible
nodes.description: Survives: vacuum of space, 300°F heat, -458°F cold, 6000 atmospheres of pressure, 1000× lethal radiation, 30 years without food/water. Enters cryptobiosis — suspends all metabolism. Has been found on every continent, in every ocean, from Himalayan peaks to deep-sea sediment. 0.5mm long. 500+ million years old. The most resilient animal on Earth.

nodes.label: Giant Tube Worm (Riftia pachyptila) — Life Without Sunlight
nodes.description: Lives at hydrothermal vents, 2,000m deep, in water up to 400°C. Has no mouth, no stomach, no gut. Instead, its body is packed with chemosynthetic bacteria that convert hydrogen sulfide into energy. The worm IS the relationship. Life powered by chemistry, not sunlight. Discovered 1977 — rewrote the definition of where life can exist.

nodes.label: Thermophiles — Life in Boiling Water
nodes.description: Thermus aquaticus from Yellowstone hot springs → Taq polymerase → PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) → the entire field of molecular biology, forensic DNA, COVID testing, genetic engineering. One heat-loving bacterium from a hot spring revolutionized all of biology. Kary Mullis won the Nobel Prize (1993). The tool that reads DNA came from an organism that lives in boiling water.

nodes.label: Deinococcus radiodurans — Conan the Bacterium
nodes.description: Survives 5,000 Gy of radiation (10 Gy kills a human). Has the most efficient DNA repair mechanism known. Can reassemble its genome from hundreds of fragments. Named 'the world's toughest bacterium' by the Guinness Book of Records. If nuclear war happens, this bacterium won't notice.

nodes.label: Honeybee (Apis mellifera) — The Superorganism
nodes.description: A colony is a superorganism: 50,000 individuals acting as one entity. Waggle dance communicates distance and direction to flowers (Karl von Frisch, Nobel 1973). Pollinate $15 billion of US crops annually. Colony Collapse Disorder threatens global food security. One in three bites of food depends on bee pollination.

nodes.label: Monarch Butterfly (Danaus plexippus) — The 3,000-Mile Migration
nodes.description: Migrates 3,000 miles from Canada to Mexico — but no single butterfly completes the round trip. It takes 4-5 generations. Great-great-grandchildren return to the same trees their ancestors left. Navigation encoded in genes, not learned. The migration IS the organism — spread across generations.

nodes.label: Hummingbirds (Trochilidae) — The Impossible Bird
nodes.description: 360+ species. Heart beats 1,200×/min. Wings beat 80×/sec. Only birds that can fly backwards. Highest metabolism of any animal (need to eat every 10-15 minutes or die). Enter torpor at night to survive. Coevolved with tubular flowers — each species fits a specific flower shape. The most extreme vertebrate metabolism on Earth.

nodes.label: Pollinating Bats (Chiroptera) — The Night Shift
nodes.description: 300+ species pollinate flowers (mostly tropical). Mexican long-nosed bat pollinates agave → without bats, no tequila. Fruit bats disperse seeds for 300+ plant species including bananas, mangoes, cashews. They're the night crew doing what bees do by day. Remove bats → lose tropical agriculture.

nodes.label: Saprophytic Fungi — The Recyclers of Death
nodes.description: Without fungi, dead trees would pile up and lock away all carbon and nutrients forever. Fungi break cellulose and lignin — the two most abundant organic molecules on Earth. Before fungi evolved to decompose wood (360 MYA), dead trees didn't rot — they became coal. The Carboniferous period ended when fungi learned to eat wood. Fungi invented recycling.

nodes.label: Earthworm (Lumbricina) — Darwin's Last Book
nodes.description: Darwin's final book (1881): 'The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms.' He estimated earthworms turn over 18 tonnes of soil per acre per year. They aerate soil, mix organic matter, create channels for water and roots. Darwin called them 'the most important animal in the history of the world.' He was right.

nodes.label: Termites (Isoptera) — The Carbon Processors
nodes.description: Process more dead wood than any other organism group. Their mounds are architectural marvels — natural ventilation systems maintaining constant temperature and humidity. Gut bacteria (not the termites themselves) digest cellulose. A termite is a walking fermentation chamber. Global termite biomass: ~450 million tonnes (outweighs all humans).

nodes.label: Vultures (Accipitridae/Cathartidae) — The Cleanup Crew
nodes.description: Stomach acid pH < 1 — they sterilize anthrax, botulism, cholera. Without vultures, carcasses rot, feral dogs multiply, rabies spreads. India lost 99% of its vultures to diclofenac (anti-inflammatory given to cattle) — rabies cases surged, killing an estimated 47,000 people. The extinction of vultures killed humans. Ecological backscatter measured in human deaths.

nodes.label: Clownfish + Sea Anemone — Classic Mutualism
nodes.description: Clownfish is immune to anemone's sting (mucus coating). Fish gets protection; anemone gets food scraps and better water circulation. Neither survives well alone. Finding Nemo is a documentary about mutualism.

nodes.label: Lichen — Fungus + Alga/Cyanobacterium
nodes.description: A fungus and a photosynthetic partner so intertwined they look like one organism. First to colonize bare rock after glaciers retreat, after volcanoes cool. They CREATE soil from nothing — dissolving rock with acid while photosynthesizing. Pioneer species. The first relationship on bare stone.

nodes.label: Oxpecker + Buffalo/Rhino — Cleaner Mutualism
nodes.description: Oxpeckers eat ticks and parasites off large mammals. The mammal gets cleaned; the bird gets fed. But oxpeckers also drink blood from wounds — the line between mutualism and parasitism blurs. The relationship is complicated. Like most relationships.

nodes.label: Mitochondria — The Enslaved Bacterium Inside Every Cell
nodes.description: ~2 billion years ago, a larger cell engulfed an alpha-proteobacterium but didn't digest it. The bacterium became the mitochondrion — the powerhouse of the cell. Still has its own DNA (inherited only from mother). Lynn Margulis proposed endosymbiotic theory (1967), was ridiculed, then proven right. EVERY complex cell on Earth is a symbiotic partnership. You are not one organism — you are a merger.

nodes.label: Chloroplast — The Captured Cyanobacterium
nodes.description: Same story as mitochondria, different bacterium. A eukaryote engulfed a cyanobacterium → chloroplast. Still has its own DNA. This is why plants can photosynthesize — they have captured solar-powered bacteria inside every cell. Endosymbiosis happened at least twice → all complex life is built from mergers, not competition.

nodes.label: The Human Microbiome — 38 Trillion Partners
nodes.description: 38 trillion bacterial cells, 10,000 species. They train your immune system, synthesize vitamins (K, B12), produce neurotransmitters (90% of serotonin is made in the gut), protect against pathogens, influence mood and behavior. You are a walking ecosystem. Your 'self' includes 10,000 species that aren't you. The membrane's self/non-self classification starts here — what IS self when you're a symbiotic colony?

nodes.label: Plasmodium (Malaria) — The Deadliest Parasite
nodes.description: Has killed more humans than any other organism in history. ~700,000 deaths/year (2022). Uses mosquitoes as vectors, red blood cells as hosts. Evolved alongside humans for 50,000+ years. Drove the evolution of sickle cell trait (heterozygote advantage). The parasite that shaped human genetics.

nodes.label: Cordyceps — The Zombie Fungus
nodes.description: Infects ants, takes over their nervous system, makes them climb to a specific height, clamp their mandibles on a leaf vein, then erupts a fruiting body from the ant's head to spread spores. The ant becomes a puppet. Ophiocordyceps unilateralis controls behavior so precisely it's called 'zombie ant fungus.' The parasite that rewrites the operating system.

nodes.label: Bristlecone Pine (Pinus longaeva) — 5,000 Years Old
nodes.description: Methuselah: 4,855 years old (germinated ~2832 BCE, before the pyramids). Lives in the White Mountains of California at 10,000+ ft. Grows slowly in harsh conditions — twisted, wind-blasted, barely alive. But still alive. The oldest known non-clonal organism. 5,000 years of climate written in its rings.

nodes.label: General Sherman (Sequoiadendron giganteum) — Largest Living Thing by Volume
nodes.description: 52,500 cubic feet (1,487 m³). 275 feet tall. 36 feet diameter at base. ~2,200 years old. Not the tallest, not the oldest, not the widest — but the most MASSIVE single living organism on Earth. Volume backscatter — how much space can one life fill?

nodes.label: Hyperion (Sequoia sempervirens) — Tallest Living Thing
nodes.description: 115.92m (380.3 ft) tall. Coast redwood in Redwood National Park. Location kept secret to prevent damage from tourists. Taller than the Statue of Liberty (93m). A tree that looks down on the Statue of Liberty. Height backscatter — how high can photosynthesis reach?
nodes.location: Redwood National Park, California (exact location secret)

nodes.label: Pando — The Trembling Giant (80,000 Years Old)
nodes.description: A clonal colony of quaking aspen in Utah. 47,000 stems (trunks) connected by a single root system. 106 acres. Estimated 6,000 tonnes — heaviest known organism. Estimated 80,000 years old — among the oldest. It looks like a forest but is ONE organism. One root system, one genome, 47,000 trunks. The trembling giant is dying — deer overgrazing kills new shoots. Pando is both the largest organism and the most endangered.

nodes.label: Baobab (Adansonia) — The Tree of Life
nodes.description: Stores up to 120,000 liters of water in its trunk. Lives 1,000-2,500 years. Provides food, water, shelter, medicine, fiber. Called 'the tree of life' across Africa. In Malagasy mythology, God planted it upside down (roots in the air). The Little Prince's baobab. Several ancient specimens have died suddenly since 2005 — climate backscatter.

nodes.label: Octopus (Octopoda) — Alien Intelligence on Earth
nodes.description: 3 hearts, blue blood, 8 arms with independent nervous systems (2/3 of neurons are in the arms, not the brain). Can change color, texture, and shape in milliseconds. Solve puzzles, use tools, escape aquariums, recognize individual humans. Last common ancestor with humans: 750 million years ago. Evolved intelligence independently — convergent evolution of consciousness. The closest thing to alien intelligence on our planet.

nodes.label: Dolphins (Delphinidae) — The Social Scientists
nodes.description: Self-aware (mirror test). Name each other with unique signature whistles. Teach tool use (sponge foraging). Mourn their dead. Play for fun. Help injured humans. Complex social hierarchies. The brain-to-body ratio is second only to humans. If we measured civilization by social complexity instead of technology, dolphins would qualify.

nodes.label: Coelacanth (Latimeria) — The Living Fossil
nodes.description: Thought extinct for 66 million years (died with the dinosaurs). Rediscovered alive in 1938 off South Africa. 400 million years old — older than trees, older than land vertebrates. Lobe-finned fish related to the ancestor of all land animals. The fish that crawled onto land became us. Its cousin still swims.

nodes.label: Nautilus (Nautilidae) — 500 Million Years Unchanged
nodes.description: 500 million years with essentially the same body plan. Survived all five mass extinctions. Shell grows in a logarithmic spiral (Fibonacci/golden ratio). The living embodiment of mathematical growth. Form follows function follows mathematics follows time.

nodes.label: Mantis Shrimp (Stomatopoda) — 16-Color Vision
nodes.description: Sees 16 color channels (humans see 3). Perceives UV and polarized light. Strikes with the fastest punch in the animal kingdom — 23 m/s, accelerating faster than a .22 caliber bullet. The strike creates cavitation bubbles that produce light and temperatures near the sun's surface. A tiny shrimp that punches with the force of physics.

nodes.label: Turritopsis dohrnii — The Immortal Jellyfish
nodes.description: Can revert from adult back to polyp stage — the only known animal that can reverse its life cycle. Biologically immortal (can still be killed, just doesn't age). Transdifferentiation: adult cells transform back into stem cells. The organism that defeated the arrow of time.

nodes.label: Dodo (Raphus cucullatus) — Extinct 1681
nodes.description: Flightless bird of Mauritius. No natural predators → no fear of humans → sailors walked up and clubbed them. Extinct within 80 years of human contact. The symbol of human-caused extinction. 'Dead as a dodo.' Also a keystone — the tambalacoque tree may have needed dodo digestive tracts to germinate its seeds.

nodes.label: Passenger Pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius) — Extinct 1914
nodes.description: Once the most abundant bird in North America: 3-5 BILLION individuals. Flocks darkened the sky for hours. Martha, the last passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. From 5 billion to zero in 50 years. The most dramatic extinction in recorded history. Proof that abundance is not safety.

nodes.label: Thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus) — Extinct 1936
nodes.description: The Tasmanian tiger. A marsupial that convergently evolved to look exactly like a dog/wolf (completely unrelated). Last known individual, Benjamin, died at Hobart Zoo on September 7, 1936. The government had been paying bounties for their killing until 1909. We paid people to drive them extinct, then mourned their loss.

nodes.label: Vaquita (Phocoena sinus) — ~10 Left
nodes.description: The world's rarest marine mammal. ~10 individuals remain in the Gulf of California. Killed as bycatch in gillnets set for totoaba fish (whose swim bladders sell for $46,000/kg in China). We know exactly how to save them (ban gillnets). We know exactly why we won't (enforcement). The extinction we're watching in real time.

nodes.label: Amur Leopard (Panthera pardus orientalis) — ~100 Left
nodes.description: The rarest big cat on Earth. ~100 in the wild (up from ~30 in 2007). Lives in the Russian Far East and northeast China. Can run 37 mph, leap 19 feet horizontally, 10 feet vertically. An athlete at the edge of existence.
